item.research_question: How can single-phase, chemically homogeneous high-entropy borides be synthesized using mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering, and how do composition and sintering temperature affect their microstructure, hardness, and thermal-oxidative resistance?
item.processing_route: Mechanical alloying of elemental metal powders (Ti, Nb, Hf, Zr, Ta) in a Fritsch Pulverisette 4 planetary mill (200–400 rpm, 7.5 h) followed by mixing with polycrystalline boron (1:2 molar ratio) and spark plasma sintering (50 MPa, 5 min hold) at 1600, 1800, or 2000 °C
item.test_conditions: Microhardness measured at 300 and 500 g; gas-dynamic tests using an electric arc plasma torch (UPIM-200) with heat flux density ranging from 3.11 to 4.2 MW/m2 in an air plasma-forming gas
key_findings: A chemically homogeneous powder with low iron content (0.12%) was obtained after 7.5 h of mechanical alloying at 200–400 rpm.
Single-phase hexagonal MeB2 structure (P63/mmc) was formed during spark plasma sintering at 2000 °C.
Microhardness values ranged from 1763 to 1959 HV, with the highest hardness (1959 HV) observed at 1600 °C due to non-equilibrium phases.
Increasing sintering temperature to 2000 °C reduced oxide inclusions and increased chemical homogeneity.
The maximum test temperature without intensive entrainment and melting was 1904 °C for the equiatomic sample and 2070 °C for the Hf/Zr-enriched sample.
The liquid phase appeared on the surface at approximately 1815 °C for the equiatomic sample and 1910 °C for the Hf/Zr-enriched sample.
Layer-by-layer analysis revealed a surface layer of mixed refractory MeO2 dioxide and a third layer containing low-melting Me4O5 oxides.
item.mechanism: The formation of high-entropy borides during sintering is accompanied by large heat releases, inducing self-propagating high-temperature synthesis where particles melt and redox reactions occur in parallel. The presence of hafnium and zirconium oxides is attributed to the lowest free energy of their formation. Increasing temperature accelerates diffusion, leading to the coagulation and dissolution of oxide inclusions, while boron oxide evaporation and interaction with tooling carbon at temperatures above 1860 °C and 2000 °C further reduce oxide phases. The enhanced thermal-oxidative resistance in Hf/Zr-rich compositions is due to the formation of a surface layer enriched in refractory Zr and Hf oxides.
item.limitations: The text notes that the initial power for gas-dynamic tests was chosen approximately due to a lack of prior data on material characteristics. Additionally, the presence of a halo in diffraction patterns at 1800 °C indicates the persistence of an X-ray amorphous fine-grained ceramic component.
item.future_work: The authors state that increasing the temperature or holding time during sintering will likely lead to the complete dissolution of oxide phases.
quotes: A chemically homogeneous powder with a low iron content (0.12%) was obtained in a planetary mill by rotating the planetary disk/pots at 200–400 rpm and a processing time of 7.5 h.
A single-phase hexagonal structure is formed during spark plasma sintering of mechanically alloyed powders at 2000 °C.
The liquid phase appeared on the surface of the sample at a temperature of about 1815 °C.

Question: How can single-phase, chemically homogeneous high-entropy borides be synthesized using mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering, and how do composition and sintering temperature affect their microstructure, hardness, and thermal-oxidative resistance?. System: TiZrHfNbTa borides (specifically equiatomic (TiZrHfTaNb)B2 and non-equiatomic (TiTaNb)0.3Hf0.35Zr0.35B2). Processing: Mechanical alloying of elemental metal powders (Ti, Nb, Hf, Zr, Ta) in a Fritsch Pulverisette 4 planetary mill (200–400 rpm, 7.5 h) followed by mixing with polycrystalline boron (1:2 molar ratio) and spark plasma sintering (50 MPa, 5 min hold) at 1600, 1800, or 2000 °C. Test conditions: Microhardness measured at 300 and 500 g; gas-dynamic tests using an electric arc plasma torch (UPIM-200) with heat flux density ranging from 3.11 to 4.2 MW/m2 in an air plasma-forming gas. The presence of hafnium and zirconium oxides is attributed to the lowest free energy of their formation. Increasing temperature accelerates diffusion, leading to the coagulation and dissolution of oxide inclusions, while boron oxide evaporation and interaction with tooling carbon at temperatures above 1860 °C and 2000 °C further reduce oxide phases. The enhanced thermal-oxidative resistance in Hf/Zr-rich compositions is due to the formation of a surface layer enriched in refractory Zr and Hf oxides.. Limitations: The text notes that the initial power for gas-dynamic tests was chosen approximately due to a lack of prior data on material characteristics. Additionally, the presence of a halo in diffraction patterns at 1800 °C indicates the persistence of an X-ray amorphous fine-grained ceramic component.. Future work: The authors state that increasing the temperature or holding time during sintering will likely lead to the complete dissolution of oxide phases..
